education.title: Family Education
education.body: The full family education library is on soberhelpline.com. It opens in your browser, already signed in.

sections.title: Addiction is a family illness
sections.body: You cannot control whether your loved one uses. You can control the walls, the moat, and the drawbridge. Families recover in parallel — not after the person using is 'fixed.' Your steadiness changes the equation.

sections.title: Help vs enabling
sections.body: A useful test: does this action protect the person, or protect the addiction from consequences? Rides to a meeting, food, treatment paid to a provider — help. Cash, covering a DUI, calling in sick for them — those cushion the disease. Naming enabling is not blame; it is the first wall.

sections.title: You do not have to wait for rock bottom
sections.body: Rock bottom is just the moment consequences outweigh denial. You can raise the bottom by ending the cushioning. People enter treatment because of court dates, ultimatums, and planned interventions all the time.

resources.sub: Levels of care, family fellowships, naloxone, and 988. The finder is a public A–Z directory. A navigator can help you choose. No sponsored ranking.

items.title: Detox
items.body: Medically supervised withdrawal, usually days. It manages safety while the body clears substances. Detox is not treatment by itself — most people need a next level of care immediately after.

items.title: Residential / inpatient
items.body: Living at a facility, commonly 30–90 days, with 24-hour structure. Used when home is unsafe, use is severe, or previous outpatient care was not enough.

items.title: PHP (partial hospitalization)
items.body: Full days of treatment while sleeping at home or sober living. A step down from residential, or a step up when outpatient is not holding.

items.title: IOP (intensive outpatient)
items.body: Several hours, several days a week. Lets someone keep work or family roles while staying in structured care.

items.title: Outpatient (OP)
items.body: Weekly or twice-weekly sessions. Often the long tail after higher levels of care — not usually the starting point in a crisis.

fellowships.title: Al-Anon and Nar-Anon
fellowships.body: Free peer meetings for families and friends — not treatment placement, not a sales call. Al-Anon is for families affected by someone else's drinking; Nar-Anon is for families affected by someone else's drug use. Search al-anon.org or nar-anon.org for local and online meetings. You can go even if your loved one is still using.

naloxone.title: Naloxone (Narcan)
naloxone.body: Naloxone can reverse an opioid overdose. Narcan (naloxone) nasal spray is available over the counter at pharmacies nationwide. Keep it at home if opioids (including fentanyl in other drugs) may be involved. Call 911 as you administer it. This is harm reduction, not a treatment plan.

lifeline.title: 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline
lifeline.body: Call or text 988 for suicidal thoughts, self-harm, or a mental-health crisis. 911 is for a life-threatening emergency or overdose (unresponsive, blue lips, stopped breathing). Both stay above any coaching or paid door in this app.

faq.sub: What almost every family asks, answered straight.

items.q: Is it addiction, or just a phase?
items.a: Look at consequences, not amount. Using despite mounting damage (job trouble, broken trust, health scares, missing money) is the signal. You don't need to be sure it's "addiction." If their use hurts your family, that's reason enough to get support.

items.q: What do detox, residential, PHP, IOP, and outpatient actually mean?
items.a: Levels of care, most to least intensive. Detox: medically supervised withdrawal (days). Residential: living at a facility (usually 30–90 days). PHP: full treatment days, sleeping at home. IOP: a few hours, several days a week. Outpatient: weekly sessions. Most people step down as they stabilize; where to start depends on safety, substance, and history.

Often, at least partly: parity laws make most plans cover addiction treatment like other medical care. Call the number on the insurance card and ask about "substance use disorder benefits," or let a treatment center check for free. Ask about deductibles, in-network facilities, and prior authorization first.

Refusal is a stage, not a verdict; most people in treatment said no first. Your leverage is consistency: clear boundaries, consequences you keep, calm repeated invitations. A professional intervention is built for this moment. And get support now, without waiting for their yes: families recover in parallel.

Ask: does this protect the person, or protect the addiction from consequences? Rides to a meeting, food, treatment costs: help. Paying debts, calling in sick for them, covering up incidents: that cushions the addiction. Enabling comes from love and fear. Naming it isn't blame; it's the first boundary.

Cash almost always becomes the substance, whatever the reason given. Say no to money and yes to the need: pay the pharmacy, bring groceries, pay treatment fees to the provider. "I love you, and I don't give cash" is a complete sentence.

items.q: What actually happens in an intervention?
items.a: Not an ambush: a planned, rehearsed, loving conversation. Family members read letters about what they've seen, what they feel, and what they're asking, with treatment ready beforehand. A professional interventionist handles the room, the objections, and the follow-through. Most well-planned interventions end with the person accepting help.

items.q: They relapsed after treatment. Did it fail?
items.a: Relapse is common, as in other chronic conditions. It means the plan needs adjusting, not that treatment was wasted or your loved one is hopeless. What matters most is how fast they reconnect to support. Hold your boundaries, skip the shame, and ask what needs to change this time.

items.q: What do we tell the kids?
items.a: More than you think, sized to their age. Kids sense something is wrong; silence teaches them to doubt what they see. Use the "Seven Cs": they didn't Cause it, can't Control it, can't Cure it, but can learn to Cope, Communicate, make good Choices, and Celebrate themselves. Keep routines steady and welcome their questions.

items.q: Do we have to wait for rock bottom?
items.a: No, that's a damaging myth. "Rock bottom" is just when consequences outweigh denial, and you can raise it by ending the cushioning. People enter treatment through court dates, ultimatums, and interventions all the time, and do as well as anyone. Waiting risks the one bottom you can't come back from.

items.q: Why do I need support? I'm not the one using.
items.a: Addiction is a family illness: living with it pulls you into vigilance, crisis mode, and self-neglect. Your steadiness is also your strongest influence on your loved one. Groups, coaching, and your daily check-in here aren't extras. They're your treatment.

Call 911 for overdose signs: unresponsive, blue lips, slow or stopped breathing, gurgling. Call or text 988 for any talk of suicide or self-harm. Don't wait to be sure; wrong and safe beats right and late. Save both numbers now. If opioids may be involved, keep naloxone (Narcan) at home; Narcan nasal spray is sold over the counter at pharmacies nationwide.

items.q: They've been arrested. Should we bail them out?
items.a: Not right away. They're scared and uncomfortable, but safe. Breathe. No treatment plan yet? Make one now, with a program that meets their needs, not just their insurance (a session with Matt Brown can help). Then make treatment the condition: bail only if they go straight from jail to treatment, no stop at home. If they back out, the family can revoke the bond, but confirm first: a bail bond agent can usually return them to custody; cash bail often can't be undone. Once they're in treatment, bring in an attorney or public defender. Tell jail medical staff about withdrawal risk or suicide talk. Don't discuss the case on jail calls; they're recorded. Crisis Mode has the full plan. Not legal advice.

items.q: Can we make them go to treatment?
items.a: Sometimes. Most states have a civil commitment law for addiction (Florida's Marchman Act, Kentucky's Casey's Law, Massachusetts' Section 35), but rules vary widely. Usually a family member petitions a court, there's an evaluation, and you must show danger to self or others or an inability to care for themselves. Stays are often short; some states have no such law. A criminal court can also order treatment through drug court or diversion. Ask a local attorney or the county court clerk how it works where you live. Many families reach the same goal through a planned, professional intervention instead; a Sober Helpline coach can help you weigh it. This is general information, not legal advice.

items.q: Can we ask the prosecutor for treatment instead of jail?
items.a: Yes, and ask in writing. The Tools tab has a letter asking the prosecutor to let them enter the treatment your family arranged and complete it, with written progress updates from the program, then an in-person meeting to decide whether the charges should continue or be reduced. Give it to the defense attorney first, and don't write about what happened: anything in writing can be used in the case. The program can send updates only after your loved one signs a release. This is general information, not legal advice.

items.q: Isn't medication just trading one drug for another?
items.a: No, though it's a fair question. For opioid addiction, buprenorphine (Suboxone), methadone, and naltrexone (Vivitrol) are proven treatments; buprenorphine or methadone taken as prescribed cuts the risk of dying from an overdose roughly in half. At a stable prescribed dose they don't produce a high. They quiet cravings and withdrawal so people can work, parent, and do the rest of recovery. For alcohol, naltrexone and acamprosate can reduce cravings. Medication works best with counseling and support. Ask programs whether they offer or allow it, and leave the choice of medication to a doctor. This is general information, not medical advice.
